## Matthew 3: research notes

**v. 1**
- "In those days" means while Jesus was still living at Nazareth. A "wilderness" in the New Testament usually means thinly farmed land, but here it was truly barren. (Wesley) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- The Judean wilderness had towns and villages in it. John didn't preach to empty desert. (Gill and Benson, quoted on the verse page) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-1.htm
- John was called "the Baptist" either because he was the first to baptize penitents at God's command, or because God started baptism through him. (Benson) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-1.htm
- Gill cites Jewish sources suggesting John was the first to practise this kind of baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html
- John's name was already well known to readers. Josephus uses the same title for him. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- This happened roughly 30 years after chapter 2. "In those days" is a general linking phrase. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-3.html

**v. 2**
- Traditional reading: to repent is to act and change direction, not just to feel sorry. John's main news was that the King was coming, and repentance was the response to it. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/
- The Greek word means a change of mind and purpose. The English "repent," which comes from a word for pain, doesn't fully capture it. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-2.htm
- The Greek tense is an ongoing command. The Hebrew idea is changing your actions; the Greek idea is changing your mind. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-3
- **Where traditions differ on "the kingdom of heaven":**
  - *Reformed (Calvin):* the Gospel has two parts, forgiveness of sins and repentance. The kingdom means God reconciling people to himself by free adoption and forgiveness, and healing them of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-3.html
  - *Baptist (Gill):* not the future kingdom of glory, nor inner grace, but the Messiah's kingdom, i.e. the Gospel age that was about to begin. John was also quietly attacking the idea of being justified by works. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html
  - *Methodist (Wesley):* the kingdom is enjoyed on earth as well as in heaven. Usually it covers both the church on earth and the state of glory. The demand to repent showed it was a spiritual kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
  - *Barnes:* best rendered "the reign of God draws near." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-2.htm
  - *Dispensational:* the Greek verb means "draw near," not "be here." (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-3.html. Havner, quoted by Precept Austin, adds that a visible kingdom is still to come, and the site's editor notes this means a 1,000-year reign. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-3-commentary

**v. 3**
- These are Matthew's words, not John's, though John used the same verse of himself (John 1:23). (Ellicott) The picture is of an eastern conqueror's herald calling for a road to be built. Spiritually, it means bringing down pride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- *Calvin:* in Isaiah the words first addressed Cyrus and the Persians, and the return from exile was a foreshadowing of redemption. "Wilderness" also pictures the nation's ruin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-3.html
- Benson: Isaiah spoke first of the return from Babylon, as a picture of the greater deliverance from sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-3.htm
- In Isaiah 40:3 "the Lord" is YHWH, and here the title is applied to Jesus. This is one way the New Testament asserts Jesus' deity. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-3
- NET note: "make paths straight" probably means getting ready through repentance. https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3

**v. 4**
- John's ministry was modelled on Elijah's. His rough clothing and food rebuked spiritual softness (Carson, quoted). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/
- Wesley: the coarse clothing suited his message, and the leather belt is like Elijah's. Locusts were clean food (Leviticus 11:22), and he ate wild honey when there were none. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- Gill rejects the ideas that "locusts" meant crabs or plants. They were real locusts, allowed by the Law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html

**v. 5**
- "All the region around the Jordan" covers the whole river valley, including parts of Peraea, Samaria and Galilee. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- The wording is deliberate exaggeration for emphasis. (Coffman) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/matthew-3.html. bible.org says the same, and adds that it shows how hungry people were for God. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-3
- It was a widespread revival, with influence that lasted for decades (France, quoted; Acts 18–19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/

**v. 6**
- Individuals confessing their own sins was something new in Israel (Bruce, quoted). The confession is what gave the washing its meaning (Spurgeon). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-3-commentary-spurgeon
- The Greek tense means a continuous stream of baptisms. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- **Where traditions differ on how people were baptized:**
  - *Ellicott (Anglican):* the baptism was an immersion, usually in running water. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
  - *Wesley (Methodist):* such huge crowds could hardly have been fully immersed, modestly or safely. More likely John poured water on their heads as they stood in rows, which better pictured the Spirit being poured out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
  - *Barnes:* a Jew might think of dipping, but the word doesn't require full immersion, and the New Testament nowhere commands one mode. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/matthew-3.html
  - *Gill (Baptist):* baptism pictures Christ's death and resurrection (Romans 6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html
  - Churches of Christ writers go further (see vv. 11 and 16).

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: it's unclear why the two parties came. Perhaps they were swept along by the crowd, or wanted to control the movement. Either way there was no repentance. "Who warned you" is better translated "who taught you?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- The viper image means hidden poison behind a smooth surface, possibly the "seed of the serpent" (Genesis 3:15). (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/3.htm
- **Where commentators differ on "the coming wrath":**
  - *Gill:* not hell, but the national disaster that later fell on the Jewish people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html
  - *Spurgeon:* God's wrath, partly at death and fully at the judgment, lasting for ever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/matthew-3.html
  - *Matthew Henry:* future wrath, beyond the present judgments. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_003.cfm

**v. 8**
- The fruit shows a repentance already professed; it doesn't lead up to it. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- Wesley separates "legal" repentance from "evangelical" repentance, which is a change of heart and life from all sin to all holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- Repentance is known by good works, as a tree is known by its fruit. (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html
- NET: the fruit is the deeds that show a changed heart. https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3

**v. 9**
- People believed descent from Abraham guaranteed Paradise. John probably pointed at the Jordan pebbles. The verse holds the seed of the later teaching that Gentiles would be called. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-9.htm
- *Calvin:* God will raise up a new seed of Abraham elsewhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-3.html
- *Baptist difference (Gill):* being born to believing parents doesn't entitle anyone to water baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-3.html
- NET: physical descent won't save anyone from the end-time wrath. https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3

**v. 10**
- Trees are an Old Testament picture of people and nations (Isaiah 5; Jeremiah 11). Pruning was a partial judgment; an axe at the root means it's now save or destroy. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- Wesley pictures a woodman who has put his axe down to take off his coat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- Coffman applies it to the destruction of Jewish national institutions under Titus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/matthew-3.html
- Constable: eternal loss for individuals, and the postponement of the kingdom for the nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-3.html

**v. 11**
- John's baptism went no further than repentance; Christ is "mightier" both to save and to judge. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/3.htm
- Carrying sandals was one of a slave's lowliest jobs. (NET) https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3
- **Where commentators differ on "Spirit and fire":**
  - *Pulpit:* one baptism seen from two sides; the fire is purification (Malachi 3:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/3.htm
  - *Wesley:* Christ fills people with the Spirit and sets their hearts on fire with love, seen visibly at Pentecost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
  - *France (quoted by Guzik):* real cleansing, in contrast to John's outward sign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/
  - *Constable (dispensational):* the fire is judgment on unrepentant Israel, mainly at the Second Coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-3.html
  - *Barnes:* warmth and purification. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/matthew-3.html
  - NET says interpretations differ on whether one or two baptisms are meant; the excerpt is cut off there. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62168/
- **Baptism disputes:**
  - *Gill:* read "in water." The preposition means place, not instrument, and the KJV wording leans towards pouring. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/3-11.htm
  - *Trapp (Puritan):* "Baptism saveth" (1 Peter 3:21) means it is effective to seal the promises whenever we repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/matthew-3.html

**v. 12**
- A winnowing fork tosses grain so the wind blows the chaff away. (NET) https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3
- Wesley: the fork is the Gospel and the floor is the church, now a mixture of wheat and chaff. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- Trapp: the fire is metaphorical but endless, and burns without consuming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/matthew-3.html

**vv. 13–14**
- Jesus came by his own choice. Guzik rejects old stories that his family pushed him into it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/
- **Disagreement:** France (quoted by Guzik) reads John as saying "I need your Spirit-and-fire baptism." Constable thinks that unlikely, and adds that John didn't know Jesus was Messiah until after the baptism (John 1:31–34). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/ and https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3
- Matthew Henry: even John, born of a woman, needed cleansing like others of Adam's line. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_003.cfm

**v. 15 (what "fulfil all righteousness" means)**
- *Guzik:* a step in Jesus identifying with sinners, leading to the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-3/
- *Wesley:* God's messengers should keep all his ordinances, so Christians should be careful to keep commands that rest only on God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- *Spurgeon:* as Head of the church, it was fitting that he be as his members are. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-3-commentary-spurgeon
- *Ryrie (quoted):* Jesus met the righteous requirements of Israel's Messiah while identifying with sinners. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62168/
- *Pulpit homiletics:* Jesus acted as our Surety (guarantor), taking our sin. Separately, the Pulpit exposition asks whether Jesus knew this was the start of his public office. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/matthew-3.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/3.htm

**v. 16**
- The Spirit isn't a dove; it came down in a visible form like one. (NET) https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3
- Wesley: possibly a glorious fire-like appearance, maybe dove-shaped. It was a visible sign of Jesus being anointed for his work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm
- The Spirit staying on Jesus doesn't mean a visible halo; it means ongoing empowerment (Isaiah 11:2). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62168/
- Only God opens heaven. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-3
- *Restorationist (Churches of Christ):* "went up out of the water" points to immersion as the only biblical form. (Coffman) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/matthew-3.html. Another writer rejects sprinkling and pouring outright. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-3.html

**v. 17**
- The Father speaks, the Son is spoken to and the Spirit descends: all three persons of the Trinity are shown. (Wesley; Constable) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/3.htm and https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3
- The words echo Isaiah 42:1 and possibly Genesis 22:2 (Isaac as the beloved son); "Son of God" is a title for the Messiah. https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3
- Mark and Luke have "You are," addressed to Jesus. Matthew's "This is" speaks to the onlookers. https://netbible.org/bible/Matthew+3 and https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-3
- Background: the rabbis' idea of a *bath kol*, a voice from heaven confirming God's choice. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-3
- Trapp notes that early writers (Irenaeus, Tertullian, Augustine) read "well pleased" as "well thought of." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/matthew-3.html
